pages.title: RFC 9110 Explained: Safe & Idempotent HTTP Methods
passages: # RFC 9110 Explained: Safe & Idempotent HTTP Methods
A practical guide to safe, idempotent, and cacheable HTTP methods, with examples and links to the official RFC 9110 sections.
4. [Safe Methods (Section 9.2.1)](#safe)
5. [Idempotent Methods (Section 9.2.2)](#idempotent)
6. [Methods and Caching (Section 9.2.3)](#caching)
[RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110) is the IETF standard that defines HTTP semantics.
The IETF published it in June 2022 as Internet Standard STD 97.
Roy Fielding, Mark Nottingham, and Julian Reschke edited it.
Roy Fielding also wrote the 2000 dissertation that defined REST.
RFC 9110 defines what HTTP messages mean, and not how a particular version transmits them.
The same semantics apply to HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3.
A safe method does not request a state change.
An idempotent method has the same intended effect when a client repeats an identical request.
For REST API work, three parts of RFC 9110 matter most.
Section 9.2 classifies methods as safe, idempotent, or cacheable.
Section 9.3 defines each method.
## What Is a Target Resource in RFC 9110?
A resource is the thing an HTTP request addresses.
A target URI identifies that resource.
A representation describes its state in a format such as JSON.
An HTTP resource does not require a database row.
A response body carries a representation of the resource.
GET /books/42 HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Accept: application/json HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/json { "id": 42, "title": "HTTP in Practice" }
This table records what RFC 9110 states for each method it defines.
PATCH is included for comparison, but a separate standard defines it.
| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Cacheable | Section |
| **POST** | No | No | Conditional | 9.3.3 |
| **PUT** | No | Yes | No | 9.3.4 |
| **DELETE** | No | Yes | No | 9.3.5 |
\*RFC 5789 defines PATCH, not RFC 9110.
A server can make PATCH idempotent by design, but the standard does not require it.
## Safe Methods (Section 9.2.1)
The rule constrains what the client asks for, not what the server records.
## Idempotent Methods (Section 9.2.2)
A method is idempotent when the intended effect of two or more identical requests is the same as the effect of one request.
[Section 9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2) states that **PUT**, **DELETE**, and the safe request methods are idempotent.
The safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE.
The complete idempotent set is therefore **GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, and DELETE**. **POST** and **CONNECT** are not idempotent.

# Idempotent: the resource holds the same value after one request or ten PUT /users/123 { "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" } # Idempotent: after the first request the resource is gone and stays gone DELETE /users/123 # NOT idempotent: each request creates another user POST /users { "name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com" }
Idempotency is what makes a retry safe.
If a network failure hides the response to a PUT or a DELETE, the client can send the request again without risk.
A retried POST creates a duplicate, so POST needs an [idempotency key](/idempotency) to become safe to retry.
A server can log each request separately or keep a revision history for every idempotent request.
## Methods and Caching (Section 9.2.3)
* **POST** — cacheable only with explicit freshness information and a `Content-Location` header field equal to the target URI
* **PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, TRACE** — responses are not cacheable
A cached POST response can satisfy a later GET or HEAD request for the same URI.
| 9.3.3 | POST | Process the content as the resource semantics define |
| 9.3.4 | PUT | Replace the state of the target resource |
| 9.3.5 | DELETE | Remove the association between the target and its function |
| 9.3.8 | TRACE | Request a loop-back of the request message |
Our [HTTP methods guide](/http-methods) covers each of these with request and response examples.
The [OPTIONS deep dive](/http-methods-options) covers CORS preflight in detail.
This causes a common error.
Developers look for PATCH in Section 9.3, do not find it, and conclude that PATCH is non-standard.
PATCH is standard.
A server can design an idempotent PATCH.
Our [PATCH deep dive](/http-methods-patch) shows how, and covers JSON Patch and JSON Merge Patch.
## What RFC 9110 Replaced
The IETF split HTTP into a semantics document (RFC 9110) and separate documents per version.
The semantics of GET, PUT, and 404 did not change.
## Section Map
| 9.2 | Common method properties | [Idempotency](/idempotency) |
| 9.3 | Method definitions | [HTTP methods](/http-methods) |
| 10 | Message context header fields | [HTTP headers](/http-headers) |
### Which HTTP methods are idempotent in RFC 9110?
Section 9.2.2 states that PUT, DELETE, and the safe request methods are idempotent.
The safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE.
The full idempotent set is therefore GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, and DELETE.
POST and CONNECT are not idempotent.
### Which HTTP methods are safe in RFC 9110?
Section 9.2.1 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE as safe.
Every safe method is also idempotent.
### Which HTTP methods are cacheable in RFC 9110?
Responses to GET and HEAD are cacheable.
Responses to PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, and TRACE are not.
A POST response is cacheable only with explicit freshness information and a `Content-Location` header field equal to the target URI.
No.
RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, and TRACE in Section 9.3.
RFC 5789 defines PATCH separately.
Every safe method is idempotent.
PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe.
### Should I cite RFC 7231 or RFC 9110?
Cite RFC 9110.
It obsoleted RFC 7231 in June 2022.
The semantics did not change, but RFC 7231 is no longer the current reference.
## Related Topics
[### 📘 HTTP Methods
Every method with request and response examples.](/http-methods) [### 🔁 Idempotency
The status codes defined in Section 15.](/status-codes) [### 🩹 PATCH Deep Dive
The method RFC 9110 does not define.](/http-methods-patch)

In HTTP/1.0, a separate TCP [connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection-oriented_communication "Connection-oriented communication") to the same server is made for every resource request.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc1945-3):§1.3

Because of this, only HEAD and some GET requests (i.e. limited to real file requests and so with [URLs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/URL "URL") without query string used as a command, etc.) could be pipelined in a [safe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#Safe_method) and [idempotent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#Idempotent_method) mode.
After many years of struggling with the problems introduced by enabling pipelining, this feature was first disabled and then removed from most browsers.
Useful for debugging.[PATCH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PATCH_(HTTP) "PATCH (HTTP)")The request is to modify a resource according to its partial state in the request.

Compared to PUT, this can save bandwidth by sending only part of a resource's representation instead of all of it.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc5789-39)[QUERY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QUERY_(HTTP) "QUERY (HTTP)")Requests that the server process the enclosed content in a safe and idempotent manner and then respond with the result.

This is similar to POST requests, but QUERY requests can be automatically repeated or restarted without concern for partial state changes.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc10008-40)
A request method is _idempotent_ if multiple identical requests with that method have the same effect as a single such request.
The methods PUT and DELETE, and safe methods are defined as idempotent.

Safe methods are trivially idempotent, since they are intended to have no effect on the server whatsoever; the PUT and DELETE methods, meanwhile, are idempotent since successive identical requests will be ignored.
End-user adoption of the new versions of browsers and servers was rapid.

In March 1996, one web hosting company reported that over 40% of browsers in use on the Internet used the new HTTP/1.1 header "Host" to enable [virtual hosting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_hosting "Virtual hosting"), and that by June 1996, 65% of all browsers accessing their servers were pre-standard HTTP/1.1 compliant.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-52)

In June 1999, RFC[2616](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2616)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc2616-36) was released to include all improvements and updates based on previous (obsolete) HTTP/1.1 specifications.
### W3C HTTP-NG Working Group
### 2014 updates to HTTP/1.1

In June 2014, the HTTP Working Group released an updated six-part HTTP/1.1 specification obsoleting RFC[2616](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2616)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc2616-36):
* RFC[7230](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7230)–"Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Message Syntax and Routing,"[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc7230-62)_Obsolete._

* it has not been widespread since 1999..2000 (because of HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1) and is commonly used only by some very old network hardware, i.e. [routers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Router_(computing) "Router (computing)"), etc.
As of 2022, HTTP/0.9 support has not been officially, completely deprecated and is still present in many web servers and browsers (for server responses only), even if usually disabled.
It is unclear how long it will take to decommission HTTP/0.9.
In 2020, the first drafts of HTTP/3 were published and major web browsers and web servers started to adopt it.
On 6 June 2022, IETF standardized HTTP/3 as RFC[9114](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc9114-69).
### Updates and refactoring in 2022
In June 2022, RFC documents were published that deprecated many of the previous documents and introducing a few minor changes and a refactoring of HTTP semantics description into a separate document.
* RFC[9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)–"HTTP Semantics,"[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP#cite_note-rfc9110-19)_Internet Standard 97._

pages.title: Idempotency key in Node.js: safe POST retries in Express
passages: # Idempotency keys in Node.js: safe retries for POST endpoints without double charges
A Postgres-backed Express middleware, the 409 and 422 rules, key expiry, and the 5xx decision that decides correctness.
**Jason Fill** · Founder 7 min read
![Idempotency keys stop double charges.

Cover graphic for a guide to making POST retries safe with idempotency keys in Node.js and Postgres.](https://apitraffic-media.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/blog/2026/10/71abecbb-idempotency-keys-for-post-endpoints.png)
A customer on a flaky mobile connection taps “Pay”, the request times out on their side, the app retries, and your API charges them twice.
Your code did nothing wrong on either request.
The problem is that `POST` is not idempotent, and the client had no way to say “this is the same attempt as before”.
An idempotency key fixes that.
The client generates a unique key (a UUID) once per logical operation and sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header on every attempt.
The server stores the key with the result of the first attempt; any retry with the same key gets the stored response instead of running the operation again.

Below is a working [Express](https://www.apitraffic.io/express) implementation on Postgres, the edge cases that bite (concurrent retries, changed payloads, crashes mid-request), and how long to keep keys.
## Why POST needs an idempotency key and PUT usually does not [#](#why-post-needs-an-idempotency-key-and-put-usually-does-not)

HTTP defines `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT` and `DELETE` as idempotent: sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once ([RFC 9110, section 9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2)). `POST` and `PATCH` are not. “Create a payment” twice creates two payments.
Clients retry for good reasons: timeouts, dropped connections, a `502` from a load balancer during your deploy.
If you have set sensible client timeouts (see [timeouts everywhere in Node.js](/blog/nodejs-fetch-timeout)), retries will happen, and the server must be the one that makes them safe.
## How the Idempotency-Key header works [#](#how-the-idempotency-key-header-works)
The IETF httpapi working group has a [draft standard for this header](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-07.html) (revision 07, October 2025).
It is not an RFC yet, but its rules match what payment APIs such as Stripe have done for years:
| Situation | Server response |
| First request with a new key | Run the operation, store status and body, return it |
| Retry with the same key and same payload, finished | Return the stored response, do not run again |
| Same key, request still running | `409 Conflict`, client may retry later |
| Same key, different payload | `422 Unprocessable Content`, client bug |

That is only safe if your handler is transactional, meaning a 5xx guarantees nothing was committed.
If the handler calls an external payment provider, pass the same key through to the provider so their side is idempotent too.

The key must be created once per user intent, not once per HTTP attempt:

A one-person team can ship this in an afternoon for the one payment route that matters.
A ten-person team should make it a shared middleware and add “is this POST idempotent?” to the review checklist, next to [rate limiting](/blog/nodejs-rate-limiting).
## FAQ [#](#faq)
No.
A request ID identifies one HTTP attempt and changes on every retry.
An idempotency key identifies the user’s intent and stays the same across retries.

# RFC 9110:[STD 97:](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/std97/ "STD 97 contains RFC 9110")HTTP Semantics
* J. Reschke, Ed.
Internet Standard
## [Abstract](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#abstract)
The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems.
This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions.

In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-abstract-1)
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-abstract-2)
## [Copyright Notice](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-copyright-notice)
Copyright (c) 2022 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the document authors.
All rights reserved.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-boilerplate.2-1)
### [1.1.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.1)[Purpose](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-purpose)

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a family of stateless, application-level, request/response protocols that share a generic interface, extensible semantics, and self-descriptive messages to enable flexible interaction with network-based hypertext information systems.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.1-1)
HTTP hides the details of how a service is implemented by presenting a uniform interface to clients that is independent of the types of resources provided.

This allows general-purpose implementations to be used effectively in many different contexts, reduces interaction complexity, and enables independent evolution over time.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.1-2)

HTTP is also designed for use as an intermediation protocol, wherein proxies and gateways can translate non-HTTP information systems into a more generic interface.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.1-3)
One consequence of this flexibility is that the protocol cannot be defined in terms of what occurs behind the interface.
HTTP has been the primary information transfer protocol for the World Wide Web since its introduction in 1990.

This specification uses the Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) notation of [[RFC5234](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#RFC5234)], extended with the notation for case-sensitivity in strings defined in [[RFC7405](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#RFC7405)].[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.1-1)

It also uses a list extension, defined in [Section 5.6.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#abnf.extension), that allows for compact definition of comma-separated lists using a "#" operator (similar to how the "*" operator indicates repetition). [Appendix A](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#collected.abnf) shows the collected grammar with all list operators expanded to standard ABNF notation.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.1-2)
As a convention, ABNF rule names prefixed with "obs-" denote obsolete grammar rules that appear for historical reasons.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.1-3)

For example, a Web browser might wish to transparently recover from a response where the [Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#field.location) header field doesn't parse according to the ABNF, whereas a systems control client might consider any form of error recovery to be dangerous.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.4-2)

Some requests can be automatically retried by a client in the event of an underlying connection failure, as described in [Section 9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#idempotent.methods).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.4-3)
### [2.5.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-2.5)[Protocol Version](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-protocol-version)
## [3.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3)[Terminology and Core Concepts](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-terminology-and-core-concep)
HTTP was created for the World Wide Web (WWW) architecture and has evolved over time to support the scalability needs of a worldwide hypertext system.
Much of that architecture is reflected in the terminology used to define HTTP.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3-1)

For example, though the URI of a resource might imply semantics that are not safe, a client can expect the resource to avoid actions that are unsafe when processing a request with a safe method (see [Section 9.2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#safe.methods)).[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.1-2)

HTTP relies upon the Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) standard [[URI](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#URI)] to indicate the target resource ([Section 7.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#target.resource)) and relationships between resources.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.1-3)
### [3.2.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.2)[Representations](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-representations)
As a result, a server MUST NOT assume that two requests on the same connection are from the same user agent unless the connection is secured and specific to that agent.

Some non-standard HTTP extensions (e.g., [[RFC4559](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#RFC4559)]) have been known to violate this requirement, resulting in security and interoperability problems.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.3-5)
### [3.4.](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-3.4)[Messages](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#name-messages)

pages.title: What is idempotency in HTTP methods?
passages: * 2 Are you asking what "idempotent" means, or are you asking why the "idempotent" verbs are are useful?Phrogz –[Phrogz](https://stackoverflow.com/users/phrogz "304,849 reputation") 2017-07-10 21:27:04 +00:00 [Commented Jul 10, 2017 at 21:27](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45016234/what-is-idempotency-in-http-methods#comment77018067_45016234)
* Report this ad
And it's worthwhile to mention that idempotency is about the _effect_ produced on _the state of the resource_ on the server and not about the _response status code_ received by the client.
To illustrate this, consider the `DELETE` method, which is defined as idempotent.
Now consider a client performs a `DELETE` request to delete a resource from the server.
Despite the different status code received by the client, the effect produced by a single `DELETE` request is the same effect of multiple `DELETE` requests to the same URI.
Finally, requests with idempotent methods can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the server's response.
The client knows that repeating the request will have the _same intended effect_, even if the original request succeeded, though the response might be different.
> Of the request methods defined by this specification, the `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE` methods are defined to be safe. [...]
And/or **idempotent**:
> [**4.2.2. Idempotent Methods**](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231#section-4.2.2)

> **A request method is considered "idempotent" if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request**. Of the request methods defined by this specification, `PUT`, `DELETE`, and safe request methods are idempotent. [...]

> Like the definition of safe, the idempotent property only applies to what has been requested by the user; a server is free to log each request separately, retain a revision control history, or implement other non-idempotent side effects for each idempotent request. [...]
Summarizing, the HTTP methods are classified as [following](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231#section-8.1.3):
| Method | Safe | Idempotent |
| POST | no | no |
| PUT | no | yes |
| TRACE | yes | yes |
However, to prevent collisions, [`PATCH`](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5789#section-2) requests can be issued such a way as to be idempotent, as quoted below:

> A `PATCH` request can be issued in such a way as to be idempotent, which also helps prevent bad outcomes from collisions between two `PATCH` requests on the same resource in a similar time frame. Collisions from multiple `PATCH` requests may be more dangerous than `PUT` collisions because some patch formats need to operate from a known base-point or else they will corrupt the resource. Clients using this kind of patch application SHOULD use a conditional request such that the request will fail if the resource has been updated since the client last accessed the resource. For example, the client can use a strong `ETag` in an `If-Match` header on the `PATCH` request.

# PUT vs POST in REST APIs: Idempotency, Status Codes and PATCH
POST lets the target resource process the representation under its own rules, for example to create something under a URI the server chooses.
PUT is idempotent and POST is not.
If you know the URI and send the complete state, use PUT; if the server should decide or an action should run, use POST.
Published
Scope**HTTP, RFC 9110**
Create**201**
To reach a known outcome, the client sends the identical request once more.
RFC 9110 allows an automatic repeat for idempotent methods.
For a method that is not idempotent, a client SHOULD NOT retry automatically unless it has some means to know the request tolerates it, or that the original was never applied.
The collection now holds 2 records with the same body.
A client that retried without knowing the request tolerates a repeat has produced a duplicate, the failure idempotent methods rule out.
7. Same failure, same retry: PUT leaves 1 record, POST leaves 2.
RFC 9110, section 9.2.2, calls a method idempotent when the intended effect of several identical requests equals the effect of one.
PUT, DELETE and the safe methods qualify; POST is not idempotent as defined, though a single resource may implement it that way.
Record counts of 1 and 2 match a small HTTP test server, measured with curl after one and two sends.
Method

Sources: [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt), [IANA HTTP method registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-methods/http-methods.xhtml), [IANA HTTP status code registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes/http-status-codes.xhtml).
The choice between PUT and POST comes up in every [REST web services](/REST-Web-Services.html) design, and it is easy to get half right.
The fundamental difference between the two is the intent of the representation: with POST it is to be processed, with PUT it is to replace.
The text adds that the intent of PUT is idempotent, and that a service which chooses the URI for the client should use POST rather than PUT.
| PUT | POST |
| Who chooses the address | The client, in the request URI | Often the server, which reports the new address |
| Idempotent | Yes | No, as the method is registered |
| On creation | 201 Created | 201 Created with a Location header (recommended) |
Anyone who wants to change only one attribute either sends everything back or turns to PATCH, covered further down.
## Which is idempotent, PUT or POST?
A method is idempotent when the intended effect of several identical requests is the same as the effect of one (RFC 9110, section 9.2.2).
The standard names PUT, DELETE and the safe methods.
POST appears in the method registry as neither safe nor idempotent.
The same section carries a caveat about POST.
The label describes the method as defined, and a single resource is free to implement POST in an idempotent way.
A client that has no such knowledge must treat it as non-idempotent.
The client cannot know whether the server acted.
With an idempotent method it may simply send the request again, and RFC 9110 permits that.

For a method that is not idempotent, a client should not retry automatically unless it knows that the request is in fact idempotent or that the first attempt was not applied, and a proxy must not retry such a request on its own.
For POST the rule is softer: when a resource was created, the server should answer 201 with a Location header that names it.
The standard suggests 409 and 415 only in its PUT section, as ways to reject a representation that does not fit the target.
## When should I use PUT, and when POST?
Four questions settle most cases.
This is an editorial rule of thumb built on the standard, not a requirement from it.
1. Does the client know the address of the resource it is writing to? If yes, PUT is possible. If the server picks the address, use POST.
Starting a password reset is a POST, since nothing is being stored at a known address.

Method choice sits at the HTTP level; SOAP, which wraps operations in a message envelope of its own, approaches the question differently, and [SOAP vs REST](/learn/rest/soap-vs-rest/) shows the contrast.
## PUT vs PATCH: replace or change part of a resource?
The abstract states the motivation: PUT allows only a complete replacement of a document.
In the IANA method registry, PATCH is entered as neither safe nor idempotent.
RFC 5789 adds that a patch can be designed to be idempotent.
| Defined in | RFC 9110 | RFC 5789 |
| Idempotent | Yes | No as registered, can be designed that way |
Whether PATCH is faster than PUT has no general answer.
A smaller body may save transfer time, but nothing in either standard promises a speed difference, so only a measurement on the actual service settles it.
## What are the main HTTP methods besides PUT and POST?
RFC 9110 registers GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS and TRACE.
PATCH comes from a separate document, and the IANA registry lists further methods, so no count of eight or four describes HTTP as a whole.
For everyday API work, the table below covers the methods that matter.
| Method | Safe | Idempotent |
### 01What is the difference between POST and GET?
GET asks for a representation of a resource and is defined as safe and idempotent.
POST sends a representation to the target to be processed by that resource’s own rules, so it can create something, trigger an action or change state, and it is not safe.
### 02Which is idempotent, PUT or POST?
PUT is.
RFC 9110 lists PUT, DELETE and the safe methods as idempotent and registers POST as not idempotent.
A single resource may still handle POST in an idempotent way, but a client cannot assume it.
PATCH, defined in RFC 5789, applies a patch document to the target resource, while POST hands a representation to the resource for processing under its own semantics.
Both are registered as neither safe nor idempotent, which is the only thing they share on that list.
